title: Closing the Loop: The Converse to the Cyclic Vector Theorem
content: The parent file `CayleyHamiltonCyclicVectorAllFields.lean` proved the *forward* direction: every nonderogatory matrix has a cyclic vector. That direction is the difficult one — its proof uses primary decomposition over an arbitrary field and is essentially the heart of rational canonical form. This file proves the *converse*, which is structurally simpler but logically essential: if M has a cyclic vector, M must be nonderogatory. Combined, the two directions yield the biconditional `IsNonderogatory M ↔ ∃ v, IsCyclicVector M v`, completing the cyclic-vector characterization of nonderogatory matrices over any field. The header docstring lays out the four-step proof skeleton: (1) divisibility gives deg(minpoly) ≤ n, (2) cyclicity gives deg(minpoly) ≥ n, (3) both monic of degree n with one dividing the other, hence equal.
mathContext: Statement: $\text{IsCyclicVector}(M, v) \Rightarrow \text{IsNonderogatory}(M)$, where IsNonderogatory means $\mu_M = \chi_M$. Combined with parent: $\text{IsNonderogatory}(M) \iff \exists v,\, \text{IsCyclicVector}(M, v)$ over any field $K$.

title: Step 1: Cayley–Hamilton Gives deg(μ) ≤ n
content: The first half of the degree squeeze comes from Cayley–Hamilton via Mathlib's `Matrix.aeval_self_charpoly` (which states $\chi_M(M) = 0$ in matrix form). Feeding this into `minpoly.dvd K M` produces `hdvd : minpoly K M ∣ M.charpoly`. Then `Polynomial.natDegree_le_of_dvd hdvd hchar_ne` gives `(minpoly K M).natDegree ≤ M.charpoly.natDegree`. Combined with `Matrix.charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim` (degree of charpoly is the matrix dimension n) and `Fintype.card_fin`, this yields `(minpoly K M).natDegree ≤ n`. This step uses *only* Cayley–Hamilton — no cyclicity needed yet.
mathContext: $\chi_M(M) = 0$ (Cayley–Hamilton) $\Rightarrow \mu_M \mid \chi_M$ (universal property of minimal polynomial). Since $\deg \chi_M = n$ and $\chi_M$ is nonzero, $\deg \mu_M \leq n$.
relatedConcepts: minimal polynomial as monic generator of annihilator ideal

title: Step 2: Cyclic Vector Forces deg(μ) ≥ n via Contradiction
content: The second half of the squeeze is where the cyclic vector hypothesis actually does work. The trick: minpoly applied to M is the zero matrix (`minpoly.aeval K M`), so `(aeval M (minpoly K M)).mulVec v = 0` for any vector v — including the cyclic vector. Now `IsCyclicVector M v` says: any polynomial p of degree < n with `p(M)·v = 0` must be the zero polynomial. So if `(minpoly K M).natDegree < n`, then minpoly K M would equal 0 — contradicting `minpoly.ne_zero (Matrix.isIntegral M)`. The proof closes this gap with `by_contra hlt; push_neg at hlt; exact absurd (hcyc (minpoly K M) hlt hann) (minpoly.ne_zero ...)`. The cyclic vector v is essentially testing the minimal polynomial, and the only way a low-degree minpoly could annihilate v is by being zero — which it isn't.
mathContext: Cyclic-vector definition: $\forall p \in K[X],\ \deg p < n \land p(M) \cdot v = 0 \Rightarrow p = 0$. Apply to $p = \mu_M$: $p(M) = 0$ as a matrix, so $p(M) \cdot v = 0$. If $\deg p < n$ then $p = 0$. Since $\mu_M \neq 0$ (matrix is integral), $\deg \mu_M \geq n$.
prerequisites: cyclic vector definition: no nonzero low-degree annihilator on v
Matrix.isIntegral: matrices are integral over the base field
relatedConcepts: cyclic vector as 'witness' for minimal polynomial
equivalence of K[M]·v = Kⁿ and dim K[M] = n

title: Step 3: Two Monics, Same Degree, One Divides the Other → Equal
content: Once `(minpoly K M).natDegree = n` and `M.charpoly.natDegree = n`, we have two monic polynomials of the same degree where one divides the other. The proof writes `M.charpoly = minpoly K M * r` (extracting the quotient `r` from `hdvd`), then uses three Polynomial lemmas to nail down `r = 1`: (1) `Polynomial.Monic.of_mul_monic_left` shows r is monic (the product is monic and the left factor is monic, so the right factor is monic); (2) `Polynomial.natDegree_mul` gives `deg(minpoly · r) = deg(minpoly) + deg(r)`; combined with the n + 0 = n arithmetic, `deg(r) = 0`; (3) `Polynomial.eq_C_of_natDegree_eq_zero` shows `r = C(r.coeff 0)`, and since r is monic, `r.coeff 0 = 1`, so `r = C(1) = 1` via `map_one`. Final rewrite: `M.charpoly = minpoly K M * 1 = minpoly K M`, which after `mul_one` gives `IsNonderogatory M`.
mathContext: Two monic polynomials $p, q \in K[X]$ with $p \mid q$ and $\deg p = \deg q$ satisfy $p = q$. Proof: write $q = p \cdot r$. Since $q$ is monic and $p$ is monic, $r$ is monic. Degree arithmetic: $\deg p + \deg r = \deg q$, so $\deg r = 0$. A monic polynomial of degree 0 is $1$.
relatedConcepts: K[X] is a PID, so divisibility + degrees determine equality up to units

title: The Biconditional: Just Combine Forward + Converse
content: `nonderogatory_iff_has_cyclic_vector` is a one-line wrapper: forward direction uses `nonderogatory_has_cyclic_vector` from the parent file (the genuinely hard primary-decomposition proof), converse direction uses `cyclic_implies_nonderogatory` proved above. The biconditional itself is a trivial `constructor; · ...; · ...` split. But the *content* of the biconditional is profound: it characterizes nonderogatory matrices intrinsically (without reference to minimal/characteristic polynomials) — they are exactly the matrices that admit a cyclic vector. This is the bridge to companion-matrix theory: every nonderogatory matrix is similar to a companion matrix, and the cyclic vector v gives the explicit similarity transformation via the basis $\{v, Mv, M^2 v, \dots, M^{n-1} v\}$.
mathContext: $\text{IsNonderogatory}(M) \iff \exists v \in K^n,\, \text{IsCyclicVector}(M, v)$. Equivalent characterizations of 'nonderogatory': (1) $\mu_M = \chi_M$; (2) $\dim K[M] = n$; (3) similar to companion matrix; (4) admits cyclic vector. This file proves (4) ⟺ (1), the parent proves (1) ⟹ (4); together with classical results, all four are equivalent.

title: Contrapositive: Derogatory Matrices Have No Cyclic Vector
content: `derogatory_has_no_cyclic_vector` is the contrapositive of `cyclic_implies_nonderogatory` and follows in two lines. If M has *any* cyclic vector, M is nonderogatory. Equivalently: if M is *not* nonderogatory (i.e., $\mu_M \neq \chi_M$, called 'derogatory'), then *no* vector is cyclic for M. This is a useful 'no-go' result — it tells us that for derogatory matrices, the K[X]-module $K^n = K[X] \cdot v$ for any single v is impossible, and one needs at least two generators (the rational canonical form has multiple companion blocks). The classic example is the $n \times n$ identity matrix $I_n$: $\mu_I = X - 1$, $\chi_I = (X-1)^n$, derogatory for $n \geq 2$, and indeed $K[I] = K \cdot I$ is 1-dimensional, so no single vector can generate $K^n$.

title: Degree Characterization: cyclic ⟹ deg(μ) = n
content: `minpoly_natDegree_of_cyclic` gives a numerical invariant: a matrix with a cyclic vector has minimal polynomial of degree exactly $n$. The proof: apply `cyclic_implies_nonderogatory` to get $\mu_M = \chi_M$, then use `Matrix.charpoly_natDegree_eq_dim` to get $\deg \chi_M = n$. This degree characterization is sometimes more useful than the equational one — for instance, when checking cyclic-vector-ness numerically: just compute $\deg \mu_M$ via Smith normal form or by direct reduction, and check whether it equals $n$. By the biconditional, $\deg \mu_M = n$ is also sufficient (with cyclicity equivalent to nonderogatoriness). So the characterization `cyclic vector exists ⟺ $\deg \mu_M = n$ ⟺ $\mu_M = \chi_M$` gives three equivalent computational tests.
mathContext: $\exists v,\, \text{IsCyclicVector}(M, v) \Rightarrow \deg \mu_M = n$. By the biconditional, also: $\text{IsNonderogatory}(M) \Rightarrow \deg \mu_M = \deg \chi_M = n$. The converse $\deg \mu_M = n \Rightarrow \mu_M = \chi_M$ also holds because $\mu_M \mid \chi_M$, both monic, equal degree.
